title: Tesla Slips as Another Executive Reportedly Exits

https://www.barrons.com/articles/tesla-slips-as-another-executive-reportedly-exits-1537542232 Tesla Slips as Another Executive Reportedly Exits By Sept. 21, 2018 11:03 a.m. ET Text Size Sept. 21, 2018 11:03 a.m. ET
Reports of another executive resignation has Tesla slightly lower on Friday.
Where we were: A number of executives have left Tesla recently.
Where we’re headed : The departures aren’t necessarily a bad thing, although Tesla’s high profile means they’re on display.
Another one bites the dust: Liam O’Connor , Tesla ’s (TSLA) vice president of global supply management, has reportedly resigned .
People close to the company told Bloomberg of the departure, although Tesla had yet to comment. O’Conner, who previously worked at Apple (AAPL) has been at the company for more than three years, although he lasted longer than Tesla’s former chief accounting officer, Dave Morton , who recently left his position after less than a month on the job.
O’Connor would be the fifth executive to leave in just a few weeks (and high-profile Tesla short Jim Chanos says that at least 42 executives have left Tesla this year). The departures come as always-outspoken CEO Elon Musk has been behaving a bit outlandishly (even by his standards) and faces an investigation related to his ‘go-private’ tweet , among other issues .
So, is further depletion of the C-suite bad news? Well, it may not look great at first blush. Yet it can also be a catalyst for change. A 2017 study by Marta Dominguez-CC and Carman Barroso-Castro in the Journal of Management & Organization analyzed 10 companies and found that managerial change precedes strategic change, and that top “management team reorganization, even without Chief Executive Officer succession, was a sufficient condition for strategic change to take place.”
A study from the same year by Jay J. Janney and Steve Gove published in Business & Society examined the fallout of the 2006 options backdating scandal. While obviously different than Tesla’s current situation, the revelation of backdating led to many executive departures, allowing the authors to examine whether or not management turnover helped bring about closer or created greater uncertainty. Ultimately, they found that while overall market reaction to departures may be negative, departures of a CEO or chief finanicial officer “ameliorate the market reaction.” It’s also more satisfying for investors when top-level players are fired rather than resigning.
Of course, plenty of executives may come and go, but certainly Musk remains the focus: While he’s gotten more controversial in recent months, he’s far from the only CEO to act out . The real question for investors is to weigh whether the benefits he brings to Tesla outweigh the recent drawbacks (and without a calmer, stabilizing force in the C-suite to counterbalance him, this question becomes more urgent).
Yet Janney and Gove’s study also showed that “firms, by shaping who and how executives depart, may amplify or dampen the damage of existing scandalizing events.” Tesla may not be crafting the narrative around the management exodus at the moment, but again it’s for the investor to decide whether the company should be focused on trying to manipulate the optics, or if its resources are better used elsewhere.
Tesla is down 0.2% to $297.61 this morning.
